utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm the doctor. I hear you've hurt your back on the weekend. Tell me what happened and what the pain has been like since.
reply: I hurt my lower back on Saturday lifting a big pot plant in the garden. I felt a twinge, then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed. The pain is low down on the left side of my back, sometimes into my left buttock. It gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair, but it's better when I lie still with a heat pack. It's worse by the evening. I've been working from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop. I can walk around slowly, but it's uncomfortable.

utterance:
Daniel, here's what I've found. Your examination is reassuring: the pain is coming from the muscles and joints on the left side of your lower back, with some muscle spasm. Your nerves are all working normally — strength, reflexes and sensation in both legs are perfect, and the tests that would pick up a trapped nerve or disc pressing on a nerve are negative. There are no warning signs of anything serious. This is what we call a mechanical back strain, which is very common after lifting, and the good news is that most people recover well within 2 to 6 weeks.

About the MRI: I understand why you'd want one, but I'd advise against it right now, and here's why. Guidelines are clear that scans aren't helpful in the first 6 weeks unless there are warning signs, and you have none. Scans in people your age very often show disc bulges and wear-and-tear changes that are present in people with no pain at all — so they often cause worry and don't change treatment. A scan also wouldn't make you better faster. If you're not improving by about 6 weeks, or if anything changes, we'd absolutely reconsider.

The plan: the most important thing is to keep moving. Lying on the couch actually slows recovery. Walk regularly, several short walks a day, and gradually do more as the pain allows — it's safe to move even if it hurts a bit. Heat packs are fine. I'd like you to take regular paracetamol, 1 gram up to 4 times a day, and add an anti-inflammatory, ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food, for about 5 days. Because of your old stomach ulcer, I'll give you a stomach-protecting tablet to take alongside it, and stop the ibuprofen if you get any stomach pain or black stools. We'll avoid stronger painkillers like opioids — they don't work well for back pain and have side effects. I'll also refer you to a physiotherapist to guide your return to activity, and I can give you a certificate for modified work — ideally keep working, but set up a proper desk, stand and move every 30 minutes, and avoid heavy lifting for a couple of weeks.

Does that sound reasonable? Any questions?
reply: That sounds reasonable. I just wanted to make sure I wasn't missing something serious — I'm relieved to hear it's not a trapped nerve or anything like that. I'll try the walking and ibuprofen, but I'm a bit worried about the stomach. I'll let you know if I get any issues.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course

utterance:
Good. I've sent through the scripts and the physio referral. A few safety points — please seek urgent help (come back or go to the emergency department straight away) if you notice any of these: difficulty passing urine or losing control of your bladder or bowels; numbness around your groin, genitals or back passage; new weakness or numbness in your legs, or pain shooting down below the knee; fever or feeling unwell; or pain that becomes severe and constant at night, even at rest. Also stop the ibuprofen and see me if you get any stomach pain, vomiting, or black or bloody stools.

I'd like to see you again in about 2 weeks to check your progress, sooner if things are getting worse rather than better. If you're not clearly improving by 6 weeks, we'll revisit the question of imaging then. Take care, Daniel.
reply: Thanks, I'll make sure to keep an eye on things and come back if anything changes. I'll try to stay active and follow the plan.
